latin.206: CAP. III. Observata quaedam in primo & secundo Capite Tractatus, & alia laudata, alia refutata. PRIMO Capite tui tractatus statum quaestionis constituisti. Eo constituto Capite secundo digrederis ad probandum, omnes homines esse infectos peccato originali, & ideo omnibus hujus vitae miseriis mortique obnoxios. quo consilio, equidem nescio. Nam tu ipse fateris extremis verbis cap. 2. nullam ea de re inter nos esse controversiam: Et vero id ipsum Thesibus quas oppugnas probaveram, paucis quidem verbis, sed argumentis multis & validis, robore & numero praestantibus, quorum quaedam expolivisti, quaedam praetermisisti. Notavi autem inter legendum nonnulla digna observatu, vel quia vera sunt, sed causae quam agis repugnantia, vel quia tam veritati quam meae sententiae adversari mihi videntur.
latin.207: Laudo in primis quae scripsisti non procul a fine Cap. 2. peccatum illud Adami omnium malorum scaturigo, actuale & PERSONALE fuit in ipso, sed infecit naturam: & omnes homines eo inficiuntur, quia sunt ab eo secundum ordinem naturae &c. Dic mihi, amabo te, si peccatum illud personale fuit in Adamo, quo jure illud idem numero quod in Adamo fuit nobis omnibus imputetur? Tu Cap. 1. dicis Deum in verbis illis Ezechielis, filius non feret iniquitatem Patris, loqui tantum de peccatis externis & actualibus, & cum ejusmodi peccata sint personalia, personam tantum spectare. Jam autem tu affirmas hoc loco peccatum illud Adami fuisse actuale & personale. Quis non inde concludat ergo peccatum illud tantum Adami personam spectabat, nec illud ferre filii ejus debent? Quid sibi etiam volunt illa verba in ipso? opponuntur ne his in ejus posteris, vel in nobis? certe in nobis peccatum Adami non est personale, sed totius generis humani, (uno excepto Christo) commune: sed in nobis nihil aliud est quam haereditarium illud vitium, quo omnes infecti nascimur, quodque omnibus, nisi condonatum fuerit per Christum, imputatur.
latin.208: Minus commode idem dixeras Cap. 1. haec culpa unius hominis fuit, sed poena omnibus hominibus est communis &c. Hoc discrimen observas inter culpam Adami & poenam, quod culpa unius hominis fuit, poena vero communis omnibus. Nonne vides quid sequatur, nimirum poenam non respondere culpae; quippe, culpam enim non communem vindicari poena communi: poenam iis irrogari, quorum non sit culpa. Certe si poena est omnium, culpa tantum unius, omnes, uno excepto, culpa vacant, quomodo igitur puniuntur juste? Si culpa unius hominis est, nec est communis omnibus, cur omnibus imputatur? Si eam dicas, cum unius sit, imputatione fieri communem omnibus, non evades, primum enim quae mea culpa non est, ea mihi imputari non debet. Non enim ideo mihi imputatur ut sit mea, sed contra quia mea est, idcirco mihi imputatur: alioqui mihi imputatur falso & injuste. Deinde si culpa Adami mea non est nisi imputatione, fecit me Deus Judex (cogitans horresco) sua imputatione peccatorem, non invenit: est enim imputatio judicis actus, non meus. Tolle imputationem, culpa illa vaco; mea enim non est, sed fuit unius hominis Adami: me igitur (vide quo ducat ista imputatio & mecum cohorresce) judex, hoc est, Deus fecit peccatorem ac reum, & causa est primi mei peccati, primi mei reatus. Denique de jure non magis ad me poena Adami pertinet quam culpa. Si igitur culpa ejus mea non est reipsa, sed tantum imputatione, idem etiam de poena dicendum est.
latin.209: His ego absurdis non urgeor, qui culpam volo esse tam communem omnibus, quam poenam: communem inquam reapse, non imputatione sed propagatione, ac nobis imputari, quia intra nos est. Culpa autem illa est vitium originale nobis singulis inhaerens, quam ipsam nolo proprie loquendo poenam esse ob eas causas, quas mox aperiam cap. sequente.
latin.210: Laudo etiam haec tua verba, Quemadmodum fons infectus rivos etiam inficit, & sicut radix producit surculos secundum speciem suam, malos scilicet, si mala est, EODEM PRORSUS MODO primus homo corruptus & peccator genuit & protulit filios corruptos & peccatores. Subsumo, atqui fons infectus inficit rivos & radix mala profert malos surculos ea tantummodo lege Naturae, qua sibi quodque simile gignit. Cur igitur non idem statuis de primo homine, si nos eodem prorsus modo corruptus corruptos genuit? Si lex ista naturae sufficit ad peccati originalis propagationem ante peccatum constituta & sancita, quid est quamobrem eam dei justitiae, dei judicis sententiae imputes non sine magno meo scandalo, qui sic magnam Dei justitiae fieri injuriam queror? atque hujus te rei ipsum propagationis nomen admonere potuit: est enim propagatio opus naturae, quae suas in ea leges sequitur, Deo, ut est naturae author & conservator, leges illas suo concursu conservante & constabiliente, pendent enim ex decreto, quod ordine naturae decretum de lapsu permittendo mihi videtur antecessisse. Itaque posteriore decreto rescindi nec potuerunt, nec debuerunt.
latin.211: Placet etiam mihi valde, quod hanc labem & corruptionem in omnes homines transfusam & transmissam fuisse clare nos doceri affirmas Rom. 5. 12. 14. 15. 16. 19. quibus versibus graece & latine pro tuo more citatis, concludis haec manifeste probare primum illud hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum, transmissum universos infecisse, & morti addixisse. Nam si illis versibus clare docetur in omnes homines transfusa corruptio, contendo ex iisdem illis versibus nulla arte concludi posse, primum Adami peccatum actuale toti ejus posteritati proxime & immediate imputari. Id quod haec nostra disputatio, Deo favente, faciet liquidum. Interim quid est primum illud primi hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum & transmissum, nisi inhaerens omnibus ab ipso ortu labes & corruptio ab ea, quae fuit in Adamo, numero differens? nam, neque ejus actio, quae simul ac commissa est esse desiit, in nos transfundi, neque imputatio, extra nos in dei mente facta, transfusio & transmissio in nos dici, neque inhaerens Adamo corruptio de subjecto in subjectum eadem numero migrare potuit. Memineris igitur te primi Adae peccati nomine haereditariam corruptionem insignivisse.
latin.212: Laudo denique quod hoc vitium, & peccatum appellas, & sic vocatum ab Apostolo agnoscis, & morti homines universos addixisse fateris, teque hortor ut in ea doctrina, quam Scriptura, & secundum scripturam Ecclesiae omnes protestantium unanimi consensu docent, perseveres constanter.

pass_a.206: CHAPTER III. Certain things observed in the first and second Chapter of the Treatise, and others praised, others refuted. In the FIRST Chapter of your treatise you constituted the state of the question. That having been constituted, in the second Chapter you digress to proving that all men are infected with original sin, and therefore liable to all the miseries of this life and to death. With what design, I for my part do not know. For you yourself confess in the last words of cap. 2 that there is no controversy between us on that matter: And truly I had proved that very thing in the Theses which you oppose, in few words indeed, but with many and valid arguments, excellent in strength and number, of which you polished some and passed over some. But while reading I noted some things worthy of observation, either because they are true but contrary to the cause you are urging, or because they seem to me to oppose both the truth and my opinion.
pass_a.207: I praise first what you wrote not far from the end of Cap. 2: that sin of Adam, the spring of all evils, was actual and PERSONAL in him, but infected nature: and all men are infected by it because they are from him according to the order of nature, etc. Tell me, I pray you, if that sin was personal in Adam, by what right is that same in number which was in Adam imputed to us all? You in Cap. 1 say that God in those words of Ezekiel, the son shall not bear the iniquity of the Father, speaks only of external and actual sins, and since sins of that kind are personal, they regard the person only. But now you affirm in this place that that sin of Adam was actual and personal. Who would not conclude thence that therefore that sin regarded only Adam's person, and his sons ought not to bear it? What also do those words in him mean? Are they opposed to these, in his posterity, or in us? Certainly in us Adam's sin is not personal, but common to the whole human race (Christ alone excepted): but in us it is nothing other than that hereditary vice with which we are all born infected, and which is imputed to all unless it has been forgiven through Christ.
pass_a.208: Less conveniently you had said the same Cap. 1: this guilt was of one man, but the penalty is common to all men, etc. You observe this distinction between Adam's guilt and the penalty, that the guilt was of one man, but the penalty truly common to all. Do you not see what follows, namely that the penalty does not answer to the guilt; seeing that a guilt that is not common is avenged by a common penalty: a penalty is inflicted on those whose guilt it is not. Certainly if the penalty is of all, the guilt of only one, all except one are free of guilt—how then are they punished justly? If the guilt is of one man and is not common to all, why is it imputed to all? If you say that, though it is of one, it becomes common to all by imputation, you will not escape: first, what is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. For it is not imputed to me so that it may become mine, but on the contrary because it is mine, therefore it is imputed to me: otherwise it is imputed to me falsely and unjustly. Next, if Adam's guilt is not mine except by imputation, God the Judge (I shudder thinking it) made me a sinner by His imputation; He did not find me one: for imputation is an act of the judge, not mine. Take away imputation, and I am free of that guilt; for it is not mine, but was of one man, Adam: therefore me (see whither this imputation leads, and shudder with me) the judge, that is, God, made a sinner and guilty, and is the cause of my first sin, of my first reatus. Finally in law Adam's penalty no more belongs to me than his guilt. If therefore his guilt is not mine in the thing itself, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the penalty too.
pass_a.209: By these absurdities I am not hard pressed, who want the guilt to be as common to all as the penalty: common, I say, in the thing itself, not by imputation but by propagation, and to be imputed to us because it is within us. But that guilt is the original vice inhering in each of us, which itself I do not want to be a penalty properly speaking, for those reasons which I will presently open in the following chapter.
pass_a.210: I also praise these your words: Just as an infected fountain also infects the streams, and as a root produces shoots according to its own species—bad ones, namely, if it is bad—IN EXACTLY THE SAME WAY the first man, corrupted and a sinner, begot and brought forth corrupted and sinful sons. I subsume: but an infected fountain infects streams and a bad root brings forth bad shoots only by that law of Nature by which each thing begets its like. Why then do you not hold the same of the first man, if corrupted he begot us corrupted in exactly the same way? If that law of nature, constituted and sanctioned before the sin, suffices for the propagation of original sin, why do you impute it to the justice of God, to the sentence of God the judge—not without my great scandal, who complain that great injury is done to God's justice? And the very name of propagation could have warned you of this: for propagation is a work of nature, which follows its laws in it, God as nature's author and conserver conserving and establishing those laws by His concurrence; for they hang on a decree which, in the order of nature, seems to me to have preceded the decree permitting the fall. And so they could not, nor ought they, be rescinded by a later decree.
pass_a.211: It also pleases me greatly that you affirm we are clearly taught that this stain and corruption was transfused and transmitted into all men, Rom. 5:12, 14, 15, 16, 19—which verses, cited in Greek and Latin after your manner, you conclude manifestly prove that that first sin of man, transfused into all men, transmitted, infected them all and bound them over to death. For if by those verses it is clearly taught that corruption was transfused into all men, I contend that from those same verses it can by no art be concluded that Adam's first actual sin is imputed proximately and immediately to all his posterity. Which this our disputation, God favoring, will make clear. Meanwhile what is that first sin of the first man transfused and transmitted into all men, if not the stain and corruption inhering in all from birth itself, differing in number from that which was in Adam? for neither could his act, which ceased to be as soon as it was committed, be poured into us, nor could an imputation made outside us in God's mind be called a transfusion and transmission into us, nor could the corruption inhering in Adam migrate the same in number from subject into subject. Remember therefore that under the name of Adam's first sin you marked hereditary corruption.
pass_a.212: Finally I praise that you call this vice also a sin, and acknowledge it so called by the Apostle, and confess that it bound all men over to death; and I exhort you to persevere constantly in that doctrine which Scripture, and according to Scripture all the Churches of the Protestants by unanimous consent, teach.

206: Chapter III. Certain observations on the first and second chapters of the Treatise—some praised, some refuted.

In your first chapter you set the state of the question. With that settled, chapter two digresses to prove that every human being is infected with original sin and so stands exposed to this life's miseries and to death. To what end, I do not see. You yourself admit, in the closing words of chapter 2, that we have no quarrel on that point. I had already proved the same in the Theses you attack—briefly, yes, but with many sound arguments, strong and numerous; you polished some of them and skipped others. Reading through, I marked several things worth notice: some true, yet hostile to the case you are pressing; others that seem to me to clash both with the truth and with my own view.
207: I praise first what you wrote near the end of chapter 2: Adam's sin, the spring of every evil, was actual and PERSONAL in him, yet it infected nature; and all are infected by it because they come from him in nature's order, and so on. Tell me, please: if that sin was personal in Adam, by what right is the very same numerical act that was in him imputed to us all?

In chapter 1 you say God, in Ezekiel's words "the son shall not bear the father's iniquity," speaks only of outward, actual sins, and that such personal sins regard the person alone. Here you affirm Adam's sin was actual and personal. Who would not conclude that it therefore regarded Adam's person only, and that his children ought not to bear it?

What do those words "in him" mean either? Are they set against "in his posterity," or "in us"? In us Adam's sin is not personal; it is common to the whole human race (Christ alone excepted). In us it is nothing but that hereditary vice with which we are all born infected, and which is imputed to everyone unless Christ has forgiven it.
208: You had put the same point less happily in chapter 1: this guilt belonged to one man, but the penalty is common to all. You mark a split between Adam's guilt and the penalty—guilt of one, penalty of all. Do you not see what follows? The penalty then fails to match the guilt: a guilt that is not common is avenged by a common penalty, and punishment falls on people who have no guilt.

If the penalty is everyone's and the guilt only one man's, then all but one are guiltless—how are they justly punished? If the guilt is one man's and not common, why impute it to all? Say that though it is one man's, imputation makes it common to all, and you still do not escape. What is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. Imputation does not make it mine so that it can then be charged; rather, because it is mine, it is charged. Otherwise the charge is false and unjust.

And if Adam's guilt is mine only by imputation, then God the Judge—I shudder to think it—made me a sinner by His act of imputing; He did not find me one. Imputation is the judge's act, not mine. Strip away imputation and I am free of that guilt; it is not mine, but was Adam's alone. So the judge—that is, God—made me sinner and guilty (see where this imputation leads, and shudder with me), and becomes the cause of my first sin and first reatus. In law Adam's penalty belongs to me no more than his guilt. If his guilt is not mine in the thing itself, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the penalty.
209: These absurdities do not press me. I hold that the guilt is as common to all as the penalty—common in the thing itself, not by imputation but by propagation—and that it is imputed to us because it is within us. That guilt is the original vice inhering in each of us. I refuse to call that vice a penalty in the proper sense, for reasons I will open in the next chapter.
210: I also praise these words of yours: just as a polluted spring pollutes its streams, and as a root puts out shoots after its own kind—bad shoots if the root is bad—IN EXACTLY THE SAME WAY the first man, corrupted and a sinner, begot and brought forth corrupted, sinful children.

I take that up. A polluted spring infects its streams, and a bad root yields bad shoots, only by nature's law that each thing begets its like. Why not say the same of the first man, if corrupted he begot us corrupted in exactly that way? If that natural law, already set and sanctioned before the sin, is enough to propagate original sin, why charge it to God's justice and to the sentence of God the Judge—to my great scandal, who complain that God's justice is deeply wronged? The very word "propagation" could have warned you: propagation is nature's work, following nature's laws, while God, as nature's author and conserver, keeps those laws in force by His concurrence. They hang on a decree that, in nature's order, seems to me to have come before the decree permitting the fall. A later decree neither could nor should undo them.
211: I am also very glad you affirm we are clearly taught that this stain and corruption was poured and passed into all people (Rom. 5:12, 14–16, 19). From those verses, cited in Greek and Latin as is your way, you conclude they plainly prove that man's first sin, transfused into all, infected them all and bound them over to death.

If those verses clearly teach that corruption was transfused into all, I contend the same verses cannot by any art prove that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all his posterity proximately and immediately. God willing, this disputation will make that plain.

Meanwhile, what is that first sin of the first man poured and passed into all, if not the stain and corruption that inheres in each from birth, differing in number from the corruption that was in Adam? His act ceased as soon as it was done, so it could not be poured into us; an imputation made outside us in God's mind is not a transfusion or transmission into us; and Adam's inherent corruption could not migrate, the same in number, from one subject into another. Remember, then: under the name of Adam's first sin you yourself marked hereditary corruption.
212: Finally I praise that you call this vice a sin, acknowledge the Apostle so names it, and confess it bound the whole race over to death. I urge you to hold fast to that doctrine which Scripture teaches, and which, following Scripture, all the Protestant churches teach with one consent.
